chapter: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk
title: Did bebop's complexity mislead younger musicians?
summary: Horace and the interviewer agree that Parker and Gillespie had swing backgrounds while youngsters who imitated only speed lacked fundamentals.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: I would like to ask you a question, because you are, in my estimation, a great authority on things like this that we're talking about. Do you think that Charlie Parker and Dizzy, having developed that unusual style, do you think that it hurt some of our younger musicians?
Do you mean at that time? Or --
When it first became so popular.
I think perhaps so in the sense that a lot of younger musicians thought that all you had to do was play fast and loud and just, you know, --,

-- kind of thing, without really knowing what was happening. So I think it would have affected younger musicians that way, and I think that's happened definitely today, where a lot of the young musicians who are maybe coming out of rock or getting more interested in jazz, and so they heard a number of

the musicians during the '70's -- or the '60's, you know, John Coltrane and a lot of these people that knew very much of what they were doing, but it was still extremely involved music, and the young musicians that hear it just hear it and think, all I have to do is go fast as hell.

Well, you see, this is what I wanted to hear from you, because those are my sentiments too. When I said hurt them, I mean hurt them at that particular time, because they weren't aware of the fact that these musicians that were playing these riffs and things knew what they were doing, while these kids, just as you said, thought they could pick up their horns and play something fast and everything and get by, but it didn't make sense what they were doing.
These guys knew how to come out of those passages, you see.
Well, the thing is that those people had the background, and Dizz and Bird and so on had been playing swing, jazz --
-- prior to that time, and it was an evolvement out of that, whereas the young musicians didn't have anything to evolve from, so --
Right. They just hear a record or hear something, and that's Bird, man. I'm going to get this, something, but they didn't realize that Bird and Dizz
could play legitimate, you know, something that these kids couldn't, so this is what I mean by do you think it hurt them at that time.
Oh, that's okay. But I think they have become aware of this now, after they found out that something was missing. They had to get down to the fundamentals of it, you know.

Well, that's it. What I was about to say was, obviously, the younger musicians who started that way, if that's all they ever did, they never amounted to anything, and if they did go about learning what they were doing, then they had the opportunity to grow with it.
